title: Can FootPrint’s flowchart pattern work in ML?

introduction.title: Can FootPrint’s flowchart pattern work in ML?
introduction.lead:
Training changes the numbers a model uses to predict. Validation checks those predictions on separate examples. A release chooses which model an application will use.

We tested model changes, held-out data, restart and release. We also checked inference—using a trained model to predict—to see whether a worker actually used its approved model.

claims.text: The story asks whether FootPrint’s existing workflow and provenance pattern fits ML orchestration; it does not propose replacing numerical frameworks.
Retained examples cover training, model/data mistakes, recording costs, JAX, saved Lens/foottrace inspection and explicit checkpoint recovery.
The chapter sequence explains the learning from retained experiments without asserting exact project dates or runtime order.
Complete structured logs also solved the controlled diagnosis questions, and no independent human debugging advantage or production-scale result was established.

The briefing defines training as changing model parameters, validation as checking predictions on separate examples, and release as selecting a model for application use. These are plain-language descriptions of the retained workflows.

A four-agent investigation pilot compared Lens and complete structured logs on a ranking mistake and a clean control. Both supplied correct diagnoses; independent developer performance and human debugging speed remain untested.

A later real JAX experiment trains three declared candidates, rejects an injected reversed ranking with a separate selection guard, locally releases the declared minimum-error winner and reopens its saved comparison through existing Lens tools.

General FootPrint stages, shared state, decision branches and retries orchestrate the model lifecycle. The ML layer adds domain-specific references, evaluation/selection evidence and pinned release contracts; a separate local publisher validates transferred bytes and recovers an already committed publication.

The inference proof separately checks what actually produced a prediction: a worker using cached B despite independently approved A is refused, corrected A is allowed, reordered named inputs are refused and missing actual model observations remain unknown.

claims.text: The historical benchmark measured 100 runs in 20 balanced blocks across five profiles on one warm CPU sklearn pipeline.

The controller repairs the cache in the same worker and performs a new prediction using A. Matching observed identity and prediction context allow only that output reference through the application handoff.
